newsitem.title: UK: Polish C.bank chief wants single-digit CPI in 1998.
newsitem.headline: Polish C.bank chief wants single-digit CPI in 1998.

text.p: Polish central bank President Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz, who took office with inflation at 60 percent, said on Tuesday she hoped to complete her term next year with the rate in single digits.
But Gronkiewicz-Waltz said her fight against inflation at the National Bank of Poland had made her unpopular and admitted her prospects for winning another six-year term were uncertain.

Finance Minister Marek Belka has said he hopes annual inflation can be cut to 13 percent by the end of this year and into single digits by 1998. In March inflation was 16.6 percent compared with 20.4 percent a year earlier.
In an interview with Reuters, Gronkiewicz-Waltz declined to be so precise. Asked about the prospects for single-digit inflation next year, she said: "Maybe...we'll see."

But she added: "I would like to because it's the last year of my term. When I came to the bank I said that I hoped I would leave the bank with single-digit inflation. I came when it was about 60 percent a year."
Reformist governments grouped around the Solidarity trade union imposed economic shock-therapy on Poland after the 1989 fall of communism.
The policies rescued Poland from economic crisis and were widely praised in the West. But they were deeply unpopular in Poland and reformed communists regained power in 1993.

Gronkiewicz-Waltz said her role in cutting inflation had had a price. "I am quite credible but I'm not sure if I'm quite popular," she said in London, where she was attending the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
Her term expires on March 5, 1998. To win a second term, she needs to be put forward by President Aleksander Kwasniewski, a former communist, and then approved by parliament.
Asked about her prospects for staying in power, she said: "From the legal point of view it's possible, but I think it will be difficult because I kept quite tough monetary policies."
In her latest battle with politicians, she is trying to preserve the National Bank's power to supervise banks and decide monetary policy under a draft banking law.

Members of parliament have produced an alternative plan giving greater political control and limiting the central bank's independence. "I hope they won't get important support from, for example, the president," Gronkiewicz-Waltz said.

Under the draft law which the central bank and government are working on, commissions would be set up for banking supervision and monetary policy. These would be within the National Bank but include members from outside.

Gronkiewicz-Waltz said the success of this idea depended on who served. "It depends on the quality of the individuals who will be members of the commissions," she said, adding that they should be professionals, not politicians.
There should be a legal obligation only to inform members of parliament about monetary policy issues "but not to wait for their approval."

Gronkiewicz-Waltz ran unsuccessfully for the presidency in the last elections against Kwasniewski, but she refused to rule out her chances of a second term at the central bank before parliamentary elections in September.
These may produce a more sympathetic parliament by the time her term expires next spring.
"I never forecast what will happen in a year. In the meantime we have elections. We will see what will be in the future," she said.
